paragraphs.text: KHALID IBN-I-AZIZ, J.:- Through the instant Criminal Revision, filed under Sections 435 and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (“Cr.P.C.”), the petitioner, Altaf Hussain, has called in question the order dated 08.07.2026 (“impugned order”) passed by the learned District & Sessions Judge/Judge, Anti-Terrorism Court, Sahiwal Division, Sahiwal, whereby his application for interim custody (superdari) of a Toyota Corolla, Model 2010, bearing Registration No. LEB-8282, Chassis No. NZE1402047190 and Engine No. Y085268, was declined. The vehicle was taken into possession by the police in case FIR No. 341 dated 22.04.2026, registered at Police Station City Pakpattan, District Pakpattan, for offences under Sections 302, 336-B, 364, 148,149, and 109 read with Section 34, of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (“PPC”).

Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the petitioner is lawful owner of the vehicle in question and has produced documents in support of his claim. It is argued that the vehicle is lying in the custody of the police and that its continued detention serves no useful purpose; rather, exposure to the elements and the passage of time are likely to cause deterioration in its condition and depreciation in its value. Learned counsel further maintains that the impugned order has been passed without proper appreciation of the relevant facts and the governing principles of law. Accordingly, acceptance of the instant revision has been sought.

On the other land, learned Law Officer as well as learned counsel for respondent No.2 vehemently opposed the instant criminal revision and argued that impugned order dated 08.07.2026 has rightly been passed by the concerned court after properly appreciating the available record and request for dismissal of the same.
We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record with the able assistance of the learned Prosecutor for State.

The Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997 (“ATA”) is a special law, and Section 32(1) thereof gives its provisions effect notwithstanding anything contained in the Code or any other law. The same provision, however, further provides that the provisions of the Code shall, in so far as they are not inconsistent with the ATA, apply to proceedings before an Anti-Terrorism Court, and that such Court shall be deemed to be a Court of Session. The ATA contains its own scheme for the freezing, seizure, attachment and forfeiture of property, but that scheme is restricted to the matters for which it is enacted, namely, money or other property of proscribed organizations [1], terrorist property attached on the application of an investigating officer [2], and forfeiture upon conviction for the offences of terrorism financing under Sections 11-H to 11-M [3]. None of these provisions has been shown to apply to the vehicle in question, which was taken into possession in a case of murder, abduction and allied offences under the PPC; nor does the ATA contain any provision relating to the interim [1] Section 11-O [2] Section 11-P [3] Sections 11-Q and 11-R custody of ordinary case property which could be said to be inconsistent with Section 516-A Cr.P.C. In back drop of this scenario, the question is whether the impugned order can be assailed in the revisional jurisdiction of this Court. In replying this legal question, it is observed that section 25(1) ATA provides an appeal to the High Court only against the final judgment of an Anti-Terrorism Court and provides none against an interlocutory order. In Mehram Ali’s case [4], the Supreme Court held that a Special Court constituted under the ATA is a court subordinate to the High Court which must act under its supervision and control, and that the appellate power in respect of such courts must vest in the High Court. In an identical situation, a Division Bench of the High Court of Sindh, in “Niaz Muhammad vs. The State and another [5]”, entertained a revision under Sections 435 and 439 Cr.P.C. against an order of an Anti-Terrorism Court and, with reference to Mehram Ali, observed that “special courts are not to become parallel justice systems divorced from constitutional control”. Finally, the issue was settled by the august Supreme Court in “Ali Gohar and others vs. Pervaiz Ahmed and others” [6]. In this judgment, the august Court identified the two jurisdictional facts which must exist before the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 435 Cr.P.C. can be invoked at all: first, it should relate to “proceedings”; and second, the said “proceedings” should be before an “inferior criminal court”. As to the first condition, the Supreme Court held that the expression “any proceeding” in Section 435 Cr.P.C. “has to be offered a liberal [4] Mehram Ali and others vs. Federation of Pakistan and others (PLD 1998 SC [5] Criminal Revision Application No. D-08 of 2025, decided on 07.04.2026. This judgment has not yet been reported; however, it is available on the website of the High Court of Sindh under the judgments of His Lordship, Hon'ble Mr. Justice Miran Muhammad Shah at Serial No. 40 [6] PLD 2020 SC 427) interpretation, and would thus include any steps taken by the Court under the law”. As to the second, it held that an Anti- Terrorism Court is a “criminal court” within the contemplation of Section 6 Cr.P.C. and is “judicially inferior” to the High Court, the latter being its appellate forum under Section 25 ATA, and that the legislature has not expressly barred the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under the ATA.

Applying the above prerequisites to the case in hand, we find that each of them is fulfilled. First, the impugned order was passed by the learned District & Sessions Judge acting as Judge, Anti-Terrorism Court, Sahiwal Division, Sahiwal, which, in terms of Ali Gohar (supra), is a criminal court judicially inferior to this Court, appeals from whose final judgments lie to this Court under Section 25 ATA. Secondly, the order was passed on the petitioner’s application under Section 516-A Cr.P.C. for the interim custody of a vehicle which is case property in FIR No. 341 dated 22.04.2026, the case arising from which is pending before that Court; the decision of such an application is plainly a “step taken by the Court under the law” in the course of the case and is, therefore, an order passed in “any proceedings” within the liberal meaning assigned to that expression, and thirdly, the order is interlocutory in nature; it neither convicts nor acquits any accused, and no appeal lies against it under Section 25(1) ATA or under any other provision of the ATA. All the prerequisites being satisfied, the instant revision under Sections 435 and 439 Cr.P.C. is competent and has been rightly entertained

Section 516-A Cr.P.C. empowers a Criminal Court, before which any property regarding which an offence appears to have been committed, or which appears to have been used for the commission of an offence, is produced during an inquiry or trial, to make such order as it thinks fit for the proper custody of such property pending the conclusion of the inquiry or trial. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has recognized that, under the general criminal law, a seized vehicle which has become case property may be released on superdari during the trial under this provision [7]. The primary consideration while deciding an application for Superdari is whether the applicant has established a legitimate claim to the vehicle and whether its release, subject to appropriate safeguards, would prejudice the investigation, trial or any lawful claim of another person. A vehicle, being a property susceptible to deterioration and depreciation, ordinarily ought not to remain in police custody for an indefinite period when its continued retention is not required for any legitimate investigative or judicial purpose. The object of interim custody is to preserve the property and ensure its production before the competent court whenever required, rather than to impose unnecessary hardship upon its lawful claimant whose right to hold property, and not to be deprived of it save in accordance with law, is guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973. An application under Section 516-A Cr.P.C. must, accordingly, be decided expeditiously and by a reasoned order, after affording the parties a fair opportunity to contest the legalityof the seizure, and the interim custody so granted may continue, subject to bond and surety, until the final decision of the case. [8]

In the present case, the claim of the petitioner requires consideration in the light of the available ownership documents, the circumstances in which the vehicle was taken into possession, [7] Amjad Ali vs. The State (PLD 2020 SC 299) [8] Ahsan Ali Dawach vs. The State through Chairman NAB and others (2025 SCMR 1041) and Muhammad Hanif vs. The state and others” (2011 SCMR 1471). and the purpose, if any, for which it is required by the investigating agency or the learned trial court. The impugned order does not appear adequately to address the question whether the vehicle could be entrusted to the petitioner on appropriate terms and conditions sufficient to safeguard the interests of all concerned. The mere fact that the vehicle is lying in a police station, without a demonstrated necessity for its retention, cannot by itself constitute a sufficient ground to refuse interim custody, particularly when the relevant evidentiary requirements can be met through photographs, inspection, the recording of identification particulars and other appropriate measures [9].

Needless to observe that the grant of superdari is an arrangement for interim custody; it neither amounts to a final determination of ownership nor confers any indefeasible right upon the recipient. The competent court retains the authority to determine any rival claim in accordance with law, including at the conclusion of the trial under Section 517 Cr.P.C. Equally, release cannot be ordered mechanically where the vehicle is required for identification, forensic examination, recovery proceedings or any other specific purpose connected with the investigation or trial. Such requirements, however, must be assessed on the facts of the particular case and cannot be presumed in the absence of a relevant justification. Learned counsel for the complainant and the learned Prosecutor could not point out any justification sufficient to warrant the denial of superdari of the subject vehicle to the petitioner, who claims to be its owner and who, through his counsel, has undertaken to produce the vehicle as and when required by the learned trial court. [9] Ahsan Ali’s case (supra) (2025 SCMR 1041).

In view of the foregoing, the impugned order dated 08.07.2026 cannot be sustained and is hereby set aside. Consequently, the instant Criminal Revision No. 57434 of 2026 filed by the petitioner, Altaf Hussain, is allowed, and the matter is remitted to the learned trial court/competent court for the release of the vehicle in question on superdari to the petitioner, subject to verification of his ownership or lawful entitlement, completion of any necessary examination and documentation (including the taking of photographs and the recording of the vehicle’s identification particulars), and the furnishing of a superdari bond, in an amount commensurate with the value of the vehicle, with surety to the satisfaction of the said court. The petitioner shall undertake not to alienate, alter, conceal or otherwise change the identity or condition of the vehicle, and shall produce it before the competent court as and when directed. The vehicle shall remain subject to the final outcome of the proceedings and to any lawful order passed by the competent court, including an order under Section 517 Cr.P.C.

It is, however, clarified that nothing observed herein shall prejudice the merits of the criminal case or any competing claim to the vehicle. This order is confined solely to the question of interim custody. (Syed Shahbaz Ali Rizvi) (Khalid Ibn-i-Aziz) Judge Judge APPROVED FOR REPORTING (Khalid Ibn-i-Aziz) Judge Irfan Shah*
